title: The temple that was meant to last
translation: Nothing stays the same. It's like the Asuka River in the old poem, where yesterday's deep pool is today's shallows. Time moves on, things end, joy and sorrow take turns. Places that were full of life turn into empty fields, and houses that are still standing have new people in them. The peach and plum trees in the garden can't talk, so who is left to share the old days with? And the remains of great places from before my time feel even emptier.

When you look at the Kyōgoku mansion and the Hōjōji temple, you can still feel what they were meant to be, and how much has changed gets to you. Michinaga had them built and polished to perfection, gave them estate after estate, and was sure that his family alone would look after the emperor and hold up the world, for good. Could he ever have imagined it would all fall apart like this?

The great gate and the main hall were still there until recently, but the south gate burned down some years back, and the main hall collapsed after that and just lies there. Nobody's rebuilding it. Only the Amida Hall is still the way it was. Nine huge Buddhas sit in a row there, and they still fill you with awe. The name plaque in Yukinari's handwriting and the doors with Kaneyuki's writing on them still look fresh, and that's moving. The Lotus Hall seems to be standing too. How long will that last?

Other places don't even have that much left. Sometimes a few foundation stones survive, but nobody knows for sure what stood there. So making plans for everything, all the way to a future you'll never see, is pointless.

literal: Since it is a world as inconstant as the deeps and shallows of the Asuka River, time shifts and things pass, joys and sorrows come and go, places that were splendid become fields where no one lives, and in houses that have not changed, the people have changed.
Since peach and plum do not speak, with whom should one talk of the past?
Still more, the traces of the noble things of an age one never saw are very fleeting.
Looking at the Kyōgoku mansion, the Hōjōji and so on, the intention remains, and the way things have changed is moving.

When the Lord of the Midō had them built and polished, donated many estates, and intended that his own family alone should be the emperor's guardians and the pillar of the world into the far future, could he have thought that in any age it would decay this much?
The great gate, the golden hall and so on remained until recently, but in the Shōwa era the south gate burned.
The golden hall has since stayed fallen down, and there is no effort to raise it.
Only the Muryōju-in remains in its original form.
Nine Buddhas of sixteen feet sit in a row, very venerable.
The plaque by Major Counsellor Yukinari, and the doors written by Kaneyuki, look vivid, and that is moving.
The Lotus Hall and so on seem still to be there.
How long will this, too, last?
In places without even this much of a trace, sometimes only foundation stones remain, but there is no one who knows clearly.
So, to make plans for everything even to an age one will not see is surely futile.

notes.quote: 飛鳥川の淵瀬常ならぬ世
notes.text: An allusion to a Kokinshū poem: 'What in this world is constant? The Asuka River: yesterday's deep pool is today's shallows.' Every reader knew it, so the translation puts the image into the sentence.

From a couplet by Sugawara no Fumitoki in the Wakan Rōeishū: the peach and plum trees do not speak, so how many springs have passed; no one can say who lived here. The image goes back to a Chinese saying about peach and plum trees, which draw people without speaking.

Fujiwara no Michinaga (966–1028), the most powerful man of the Heian court, called the Lord of the Midō ({御堂殿|みだうどの}) after this temple. The Kyōgoku mansion was his residence, and the Hōjōji his great temple in the capital, built around 1020. By Kenkō's time it was mostly a ruin.

notes.quote: 正和のころ南門は焼けぬ
notes.text: The Shōwa era (1312–1317, not the 20th-century Shōwa). How long before this section it was depends on when it was written, which is disputed. し in ありしかど: he had seen it himself.

{丈六|ぢやうろく}: sixteen feet (about 4.8 metres), the traditional height of the Buddha standing; seated statues of this rank, like these, are about half that. The nine represented the nine levels of rebirth in Amida's Pure Land.
Fujiwara no Yukinari (972–1028) was one of the three great calligraphers of the Heian period.

notes.quote: 見ざらむ世までを思ひ掟てむこそ、はかなかるべけれ
notes.text: こそ … べけれ. The section moves from one ruined temple to a general point: planning for a future you won't see is futile.
